newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Western National sees sales rise.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Western National sees sales rise.

text.p: Western National Corp chairman Michael Poulos said on Tuesday the company was comfortable with analysts' estimates that sales in 1997 would be around $2 billion, up from $1.6 billion in 1996.
He told Reuters around 80 percent of sales would come in Western National's fast-growing proprietary annuities, which it markets in conjunction with selected financial institutions.
"The street's got us pegged at about $2 billion (in sales for 1997) and at this point we certainly don't see any argument with that," Poulos said.
Poulos said the firm ended 1996 in partnership with 10 financial institutions to sell the proprietary annuities, but it expected that number to grow.
"Yes, as we speak we're working on them. We're being very selective, we would like to deal with medium to large institutions," he said.
The firm's propriety annuities are sold through the institutions, who then manage the money from sales in a partnership that Poulos said is unique in the insurance industry.

Earnings estimates for 1997 range from $1.70 to $1.90 a share. Poulos said the company would probably earn "someplace in between" those two numbers, but was not more specific. Net earnings for 1996 were $1.53 a share.

Western National began the proprietary annuities program three years ago and, according to one industry ranking, ended 1996 as the nation's top underwriter in its niche. Poulos expected competitors to adopt a similar strategy of linking up with financial institutions, but "it's going to take them a lot to catch up."
"The life insurance companies have been treating banks like enemies. We saddled up and said, 'hell, lets go down the aisle together.' Frankly, this is the way the business is now going," he said.

Poulos said Western National, which is 46 percent owned by insurance giant American General Corp, would continue to concentrate on the sale of fixed annuities because baby boomers worried about retirement provide a growing market.
"We won't try to muddy the water by adding more products," he said.
Poulos said it was also unlikely the company, now with more than $10 billion in assets, would seek acquisitions.
"We're growing at a very rapid clip internally," he said.
Western National said its investment spread on assets widened to 2.19 percent in the fourth quarter, up from 2.08 percent for the same period a year ago.
"I'd be very happy if we hang in there at 2.19 (in 1997). That's the absolute upper end of what we've been able to achieve in the last 40 months," he said.
